chapter_title: Concerning the Fasting of the Saints
spiritual_reading:
The first work is that a person willingly lays aside the claims of the outer self and denies its cravings, so that the governing love of self and the world within him is brought into obedience and no longer rules.

The second is that the daily reception of life and understanding through outward support is to be made fit for heaven: it is to be consecrated, set in order, and freed from the falsity and evil that flow in from hell and mingle with it.

The third is that the person is to render every act an act of worship: he is to let nothing proceed from him except what accords with the pure acknowledgment of good and truth that is without taint. He must not injure the good and truth he receives by turning it to selfish ends, but keep his inner life undefiled; for those who are in this state will what is good without contamination and think what is true without distortion, and thus remain in the tranquillity that comes from concord.

The fourth is that, from the Lord’s enduring of temptations and the consequent deliverance, they take for themselves a fixed rule of life; they restrain their power in outward action from doing harm, and refuse to violate the life of another’s soul by leading it into evil or falsity. This part of the teaching is unclear in its broken phrases, but its sense is the establishment of restraint in action so that spiritual life is preserved.

fills.notes: Accepted. In the oldest substrate this fixed phrase names the Light-stock itself, i.e., those constituted from unmixed Light, which matches the following description “neither corruption nor …” and the concern not to harm the Light-substance in food.

The series requires a second negated predicate parallel to “corruption”: not only decay (mixture leading to dissolution) but also stain (adulterating contact with Darkness). This also prepares the next clause about not defiling the food.
Accepted. It states the interior condition of the Light-vessel: no foreign admixture that can pollute, corresponding to the spiritual sense of an undefiled inner life.

The fourth work begins from “the Cross” as the fixed token of endured conflict and deliverance; the required verb is one of establishing a rule or mark from it. “sign upon the Cross” gives the needed sense: they take it as an instituted standard set over their conduct, leading into the restraint described next.

The clause needs a purpose link: they restrain their hands from the hand of harming, in order that they do not destroy the living soul. “that he may” supplies the functional connection demanded by the correspondential logic (restraint for preservation of life).

assessment: Most restorations are structurally constrained by the correspondential sequence of the ‘four works’: (1) subduing the ruling power, (2) purifying what is received daily, (3) keeping the Light undefiled in deed and in food, (4) instituting restraint in outward action from the Cross so as not to destroy living soul. ¶5 #2 and ¶6 #1 remain the loosest because the Coptic idiom behind them is not recoverable from the excerpt alone; the fills supplied follow the substrate logic of mixture versus purity and of the Cross as an established rule of restraint.
